He Who Formed the Eye Sees: The Eye and the Miracle of Sight
He who implanted the ear, won't he hear? He who formed the eye, won't he see? (Psalm 94:9)

Peace to you, brothers and sisters! Let me start with a scene that has played out in a lot of homes. One morning, a grandpa is turning the house upside down. He has checked under the sofa, he has pulled open every drawer, and he keeps muttering, "Where are my glasses? Who took my glasses?"

The whole family gets mobilized to help him look. After ten minutes, his little granddaughter looks up and laughs: "Grandpa, your glasses are on your head!" Everyone bursts out laughing. Grandpa laughs too: "So I've been wearing them the whole time I was looking for them."

Today we are going to talk about exactly that kind of thing, something we use every day but rarely think about: our eyes. Every day they help us read, find our way and see the faces of our families, yet we rarely stop to say thank you. So today, let's take the glasses off our heads and take a good look at this "miracle of sight."
Engineering Finished in the Blink of an Eye

Right now you are looking at this screen, or looking ahead of you while you listen to me. Light passes through the cornea and lens at the front of your eye and lands on the retina, a thin layer at the back of your eyeball. There it turns into electrical signals, which travel to your brain and become "seeing."
This entire process is finished in the blink of an eye. You didn't press any button or give any command, and yet it takes no effort at all.

Think about it: our eyes have an "autofocus" function. The lens changes its thickness by means of the ciliary muscle around it, adjusting automatically whether we look near or far. One moment you are looking at your phone, the next you look up at the mountains in the distance, and it adjusts instantly.

It also has an "auto-exposure" function. The pupil is like a camera's aperture, shrinking when the light is strong and widening when it is weak. Walk out of the blazing sun into a movie theater, and at first you can't see a thing; after a while, you slowly begin to see. That is your eye quietly adjusting for you.
A Hundred Million Little Light-Sensing Soldiers

Let's look further in. The retina of one eye has on average about ninety-two million rod cells, which handle dim light, and about four point six million cone cells, which handle color and detail and are concentrated in a central spot called the "fovea." These numbers come from the cell counts of human retinas by Curcio and colleagues. People vary quite a bit; these are averages.
What does ninety-two million look like? It's as if a whole nation of tiny soldiers lives at the back of your eye, each holding a little light-sensing panel, standing guard day and night.

Even more amazing, in very dark places the rod cells can respond to extremely faint light. In 2016, a very carefully designed experiment reported that volunteers detected a "single photon" at a rate slightly better than random guessing. That is the result of just one study, and the success rate was only slightly better than guessing, so it needs more replication. But the mere possibility is enough to make us marvel: the human eye is sensitive almost down to the smallest unit of light.
The hearing ear, and the seeing eye, Yahweh has made even both of them. (Proverbs 20:12)
King Solomon said this three thousand years ago. He didn't know about rod cells and had never heard of photons, but he knew something more fundamental: these eyes have a source. Yahweh made them.

So, brothers and sisters, every morning when you open your eyes, you are actually unwrapping a gift. We often give thanks for big things, for a promotion, for healing from an illness. But have you ever given thanks that "this morning I can see"?
2. The One Who Truly Sees Is the One Reading the Picture
However Good the Camera, Someone Has to Read the Picture
Although the eye is like a good camera, what truly "sees" is not the eye itself but the brain behind it.

The image that lands on the retina is actually upside down, and the brain reads it right side up. Our two eyes see slightly different pictures, and the brain merges them into a sense of depth, which is why you can judge how far away a cup is, or reach out and catch a set of keys tossed to you. Each eye also has a blind spot, and the brain and the other eye fill it in together, so you never even notice.

This brings a comparison to mind. A top-of-the-line camera may take thousands of photos and store them on a memory card, but if no one looks at them and makes sense of them, those photos are just a pile of signals. The eye is like the camera; the brain is like the one reading the pictures. Seeing is the result of a whole team working together.
A Discussion About Whether the Design Is Good

At this point, some of you may have heard a certain claim. The human retina is "inverted": the light-sensing cells are in the innermost layer, so light must first pass through several layers of nerve cells to reach them. The biologist Richard Dawkins argued that this is like mounting the wires in front of a camera's sensor, an example of "bad design."

This question deserves a serious hearing. Later research brought out another side: the retina contains Müller glial cells that act like living optical fibers, guiding light to the light-sensing cells; the light-sensing cells sit right against a layer of pigment epithelium, which supplies nutrients and recycles light-sensitive pigment; in the fovea the upper cells are pushed aside, so light falls directly on the cone cells; and the inverted structure may also have a space-saving advantage.

So there are two views here. One says: light has to pass through the nerve layer first, and it creates a blind spot, so if you designed it from scratch you would not do it this way. The other says: the inverted structure gives the light-sensing cells ample nourishment and repair, with light-guiding cells and the fovea compensating, so overall it is an ingenious trade-off. As for how much the Müller cells actually contribute to human vision, scientists are still discussing that too.

I really like the humble reminder in this unit: to judge whether a design is good, we first need to fully understand what it does. It's like a little child looking under the hood of a car for the first time and saying, "What a mess! Pipes going everywhere!" But the engineer knows that every pipe has its place. Our understanding of the eye is still growing, and both sides do well to stay open.

We also need to be clear: whether the inverted retina is good or bad involves judgments about function and trade-offs, not just anatomical facts. And that the eye's many layers working together so intricately point to a Designer is a philosophical inference; it is not saying "science has proven God." But it is a very reasonable inference.
He Who Formed the Eye Sees
The psalmist answers the doubter with one simple question:
He who implanted the ear, won't he hear? He who formed the eye, won't he see? (Psalm 94:9)
That question has real power. The One who could design autofocus and auto-exposure, and who can turn an upside-down image right side up, could He Himself be unable to see?

This is a great comfort to us. The tears you secretly cry at night, He sees. The quiet effort you put in at work that no one else notices, He sees. That struggle in your heart you can't put into words, He sees that too. The One who made the eye has never closed His eyes to you.
3. The Lamp of the Body: The Eyes of the Heart
Our eyes let us see the world outside. But Jesus reminds us that there is another, inner eye, and it decides whether we spend our lives in the light or in the darkness.

The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness! (Matthew 6:22–23)

Have you noticed that different people can see completely different things in the very same situation? Two people watch a sunset together. One says, "How beautiful! Thank You, God!" The other says, "Sigh, another day gone, and I got nothing done." Same sunset, different eyes.

The eyes of our heart often grow dim. Jealousy makes us see only what other people have. Bitterness makes us see only other people's faults. Worry makes us see only tomorrow's dark clouds. When that happens, even with perfect twenty-twenty vision, our heart is still full of darkness.
That is why the psalmist prayed like this:
Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law. (Psalm 119:18)

Our physical eyes see what God has made; the eyes of our heart must be opened before we can see the Creator and the wonders of His Word. Brothers and sisters, what we need is not just a good pair of glasses, but a pair of eyes that God has opened.
The Bible Is My Standard: Put On the Glasses of Truth

Anyone who wears glasses knows that when the prescription is right, the world comes into focus. One of the three foundations of 321 is "the Bible is my standard." Before reading Scripture, ask God to open my eyes, so that truth becomes the lens through which I see everything. I don't use my own ideas to correct the Bible; I let the Bible correct my vision.
From Man's Perspective to God's Perspective

Look at the same situation through God's eyes, and you will often see grace. Your child does poorly on an exam: from a human perspective it's a failure; from God's perspective it's a chance to learn humility and hard work. You get transferred at work: from a human perspective it's bad luck; from God's perspective it may be that He wants to lead you somewhere new.
What changes is not the situation itself, but the eyes we look at it with. That is what it means to move from man's perspective to God's perspective.
Give Thanks in Everything: Being Able to See Is a Gift

Finally, let's learn to be thankful. Being able to see is itself a gift, every single day. We often don't realize how precious something is until we lose it; but we can choose to say thank you while we still have it.

This week: every night before bed, write down three graces you "saw" that day, for seven days in a row. It might be your child's smiling face, a patch of blue sky outside the window, or a cup of coffee a coworker handed you. After seven days, you will discover that grace was there all along; we just didn't see it before.

Let's go back to that grandpa at the beginning, wearing his glasses the whole time he was looking for them. Sometimes we are just like that: living in God's grace all along, and all along searching for where grace might be.

Today, let's stop. Close your eyes for ten seconds, then slowly open them. Look at the colors, the light and shadow, and the faces of the people around you, and say thank you for each one. Then ask yourself: this week, what have my eyes most often been fixed on? Has it drawn me closer to God, or further away?
The God who made your eyes is looking at you right now, and He is looking at you with love.
Lord, thank You for giving me eyes that see. Thank You for designing such wonderful eyes, so that every day I can see light, see colors, and see the people I love.

Lord, open the eyes of my heart, so that I may see the wonders in Your Word. Take away the dimness in my heart, so that I no longer see only problems, but see Your grace. And help me look at the people around me the way You see them. In Jesus' name, Amen.

2. There are differing views on the "inverted retina." From the statement "before judging a design, first understand its function," what attitude toward controversial questions do you learn?

Paving a New Road in Your Heart: The Brain, the Most Complex Organ
Don't be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God. (Romans 12:2)
Introduction: The Little Path Across the Lawn

Peace to you, brothers and sisters! I wonder if you've ever noticed that on the lawns of many parks there is a little path worn down by people's feet. The park has a lovely paved walkway that winds around in a big loop, but people are in a hurry, so they just cut straight across the grass.

At first, the grass is only bent a little. Then a second person, a third person walks that way, and after a few months it becomes a bare dirt track, clearer than the path the park designed. The groundskeeper puts up a sign, "Please keep off the grass," and people simply walk around the sign and keep going.
Today I want to tell you that inside your head there are many little paths like that. Some are good roads, some are crooked ones. And the good news of today's message is this: roads can be repaved.

First, let's get to know this neighbor who lives inside your skull. Your brain has about eighty-six billion neurons; that is the 2009 count by Azevedo and colleagues. Besides the neurons, a comparable number of glial cells accompany and support them.
What does eighty-six billion look like? If each neuron were a tree, then inside your head is an entire, enormous forest, and a forest that thinks.

Each neuron really is a bit like a tree: it has many "branches" that receive messages, and one long "root" that sends the signal onward. The junction between one neuron and another is called a synapse. One neuron can connect with thousands of others, and the number of connections in the whole brain is staggering.
An Organ with a Big Appetite

The brain has another feature: it has a big appetite. It makes up only about two percent of your body weight, yet it uses about a fifth of your body's energy. Thinking something through, remembering a face, speaking a sentence: each is the result of countless neurons working together.
So next time you come out of a long meeting feeling completely drained, don't think you were "just sitting there." Your brain was working overtime at full capacity!
You Don't Use Only Ten Percent

While we're here, let me correct a very popular saying. People often say, "We only use ten percent of our brains." There's even been a movie where someone unlocks the remaining ninety percent and becomes a superhero.

Unfortunately, there's no scientific basis for this. Brain imaging shows that over the course of a day nearly every region of the brain becomes active in turn, and damage to any small area has effects. And think about it: the brain uses so much energy, so why would the body sustain an organ that sits ninety percent idle? It's like having ten lights on in your house, paying the full electric bill, but saying only one is actually lit. It makes no sense!
In the brain God made, no part is wasted.
I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well. (Psalm 139:14)

Brothers and sisters, when the psalmist said "fearfully and wonderfully," he didn't even have a word for neuron. But the more we know today, the more we can say with him: truly, fearfully and wonderfully made.

One of the most wonderful things about the brain is that it isn't a block of hardened concrete; it can change. Scientists call this "plasticity": connections that are used often grow stronger, and those used rarely grow weaker. Learning, practice and habits are all reshaping our brains.

This unit uses a great comparison: the brain is like a city's road network. Routes that are traveled often get widened into highways, while paths rarely used slowly grow over with grass. The thoughts and actions you repeat every day are paving the roads of your heart.
Just like that little path across the lawn: once or twice, you hardly notice; walk it long enough, and it becomes a highway.

There's a famous study of London taxi drivers. London's streets are notoriously complicated, and drivers have to memorize a huge number of routes. The study found that in these drivers, the rear part of the hippocampus, which handles spatial memory, was larger than in other people, and the longer they had been driving, the larger this region was.

This is a famous example of the brain changing through use. Of course, the study shows a correlation, and the detailed causal mechanisms are still being researched. But it gives us a vivid picture: whatever you use often, your brain grows in that direction.

The brain has another beautiful feature: it divides the labor and works as a team. Seeing, hearing, moving, speaking, remembering and judging each have main regions responsible for them, yet any single task needs many regions working together. Right now you are listening to me, looking ahead, and maybe thinking about what to have for lunch, and all of that is many regions working at once.
It's a lot like a good church team: everyone has their own gifts and role, but nothing gets done by one person alone.
3. Transformed by the Renewing of Your Mind
God Made a Brain That Can Change, and He Calls Us to Change
Now let's hear what the Bible says. God made a brain that can change, and God calls us to change. The Bible says that transformation of life begins with the renewing of the mind:
Don't be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God. (Romans 12:2)
This doesn't mean the Bible is teaching neuroscience. When Paul wrote Romans, he wasn't teaching a neurology class. But the two echo each other: God made human beings able to be renewed.

"Being conformed to this world" means letting the world's ways of thinking tramp across our hearts again and again until they wear a highway. Comparison, anxiety, greed, self-pity: walk those paths long enough, and they become our most natural reactions. "The renewing of your mind" means letting God's truth begin to pave new roads in our hearts.

Here's an example from real life. A sister told me that whenever something happened, her first thought used to be, "That's it, this is going to be terrible." She had walked that road for twenty years, and she could walk it fast and without thinking. Then she began to practice: every time that thought popped up, she would stop, say a Bible verse, and pray a short prayer.

At first it felt very unnatural, like forcing her way across the grass where no one had ever walked. But six months later, she found that when something happened, her first reaction had become, "Lord, You are here." She laughed and said, "So my brain really can be repaved!"
This isn't some magic technique. It is choosing, day after day, time after time, to walk the new road.
A New Center for Our Thinking

But here is the key: we are not changed by our own cleverness. Many people make up their minds to change, and three days later they're back on the old road. What the Bible gives us is not just a self-improvement method, but a new center for our thinking:
"For who has known the mind of the Lord, that he should instruct him?" But we have Christ's mind. (1 Corinthians 2:16)

The brain is the most finely crafted tool God has given us, but a tool needs a master. A good knife in a chef's hand can make a delicious meal; in the wrong hands it can hurt people. Only when the mind of Christ is in charge can this tool fulfill God's original purpose.

We should also say honestly: whether mind, consciousness and moral sense can be fully explained by the physical activity of neurons is a philosophical question. And that such a finely tuned thinking organ points to a wise Creator is also a philosophical inference. But standing before this thinking forest, it's hard not to think of the Lord who planted it.
Change Your Mindset, Change Your Life

In 321's teaching we often say: change your mindset, and you change your life. Behavior is rooted in beliefs; only when our beliefs are renewed does life truly change. Trimming behavior alone is like reseeding the dirt track on the lawn without changing the direction people walk. Before long, it gets trampled bare again.
The Eight Steps of Changing Our Mindset
How do we change our mindset? 321 has "the eight steps of changing our mindset": information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, multiplication.

I especially want to remind you of step seven: "repetition." Repetition is exactly what paves new roads in the brain. Reading the Bible once won't change you; coming back to the truth a hundred times, a thousand times, slowly turns a new path into a highway. Very often what we lack is not information, and not inspiration, but repetition.
Lean on the Holy Spirit with Your Heart

Finally, the mind is a good tool, but don't use it to rely on yourself; rely with your heart on the Holy Spirit's guidance. One of the three foundations of 321 is "the Holy Spirit is my guide." We offer our best thinking to God, while acknowledging that real change is the Holy Spirit at work within us.
This week: choose one Bible verse and recite it every morning and evening this week, so that truth becomes a well-traveled road in your heart. I suggest starting with today's verse, Romans 12:2.

Brothers and sisters, there are many roads in your mind. Some were worn in when you were young: "I'm not good enough." "Nobody really cares about me." "I have to beat everyone else." You've walked those roads for decades, and you know them by heart.

But today's good news is that when God made you, He gave you a mind that can be renewed. Old roads can slowly grow over; new roads can slowly be paved. All it takes is being willing to return to His Word every day and let the mind of Christ be in charge.

Now let's be still for one minute. Notice the thoughts coming to mind right now, and hand them over to God one by one. And ask yourself: what thoughts do I repeat most often? What kind of roads are they paving in my heart?
Lord Jesus, thank You for making my mind, so wonderful and so finely crafted. I confess that I often let the world's ways of thinking wear crooked path after crooked path in my heart.

Renew my thinking, remove my wrong beliefs, and let Your truth become a highway within me. Let me no longer rely only on my own cleverness, but have the mind of Christ and lean on the guidance of the Holy Spirit. In Jesus' name, Amen.

The Love That Never Slumbers: The Heart, the Pump That Never Rests
He will not allow your foot to be moved. He who keeps you will not slumber. Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep. (Psalm 121:3–4)
Introduction: Please Put Your Hand on Your Chest

Peace to you, brothers and sisters! Before we begin today, I'd like everyone to do one small thing: gently place your right hand on your chest. Yes, right now. Don't be shy; the person next to you is doing it too.
Can you feel it? Thump, thump, thump. That steady beat began before you were even born, and right up to this moment it has not rested for a single second.

I know a brother who says the most faithful employee he has ever had is not anyone in his company, but his heart. He says, "I've never paid it a salary or given it a single day off, and it has never once called in sick." Everyone laughed, but if you think about it, he's not exaggerating at all.
Today, let's get to know this most faithful of employees.
Your heart is only about the size of your fist. Make a fist right now and look at it; that's about the size.

Yet this fist-sized organ has an astonishing workload. At about seventy beats per minute, it beats roughly a hundred thousand times a day; live to eighty, and it beats about three billion times. Of course, actual numbers vary from person to person; this is an estimate. While you are resting, it sends about five liters of blood around your body every minute.
Three billion beats, with no pause button, no restart, no saying, "I'm not in the mood today, I'll take a break." From before birth to the very last moment of life, it keeps working.
You Fall Asleep, but It Stays Awake

Most amazing of all, you don't need to remind it. You don't get up in the morning and tell yourself, "OK, remember to keep your heart beating today!" When you fall asleep, your heart stays awake. You forget about it, but it doesn't forget about you.
He will not allow your foot to be moved. He who keeps you will not slumber. Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep. (Psalm 121:3–4)

Brothers and sisters, if even the heart God made is this faithful, how much more faithful is the God who made the heart? The God who holds your life is more faithful than your heartbeat. Sometimes you may wonder, "Has God forgotten me?" Put your hand on your chest: every beat is telling you that He has not forgotten. He does not slumber, and He does not sleep.
2. A Symphony Orchestra Inside Your Heart
Why can the heart beat so regularly? It turns out there is a sophisticated electrical system inside it.
The first main character is called the "sinoatrial node," or SA node. It sits in the right atrium and is the heart's natural pacemaker, firing electrical signals on its own at a regular rhythm.

The second main character is the "atrioventricular node," or AV node. When the signal arrives here, it is deliberately delayed by about a tenth of a second. Why the delay? So that the atria can first squeeze blood into the ventricles.

The third group of characters is the "bundle of His and the Purkinje fibers." Like high-speed cables, they spread the signal rapidly through both ventricles, so the ventricles contract powerfully almost at the same moment.
Finally, there are four valves, like one-way doors, making sure blood flows in only one direction and never backs up.
The Conductor and That One Beat of Waiting

This unit has a beautiful comparison: the heart is like a symphony orchestra. The SA node is the conductor; the AV node is like the conductor's pause, letting each section come in at the right moment. Without that one beat of waiting, the whole piece would fall apart.

I especially love that "one beat of waiting." A tenth of a second, too short for you to notice, and yet indispensable. If the atria and ventricles contracted at the same time, blood couldn't be properly passed from the upper chambers to the lower ones.

Our lives often need that one beat of waiting too. We are in a hurry for answers, in a hurry for results, in a hurry for God to act right now. But sometimes God builds in a small delay. It's not that He has forgotten; it's so that each thing can come in at the right time.

I think of a young brother who really wanted to get married soon. He prayed for several years with no answer and at one point became very discouraged. Later he said that those years of waiting taught him to take care of his own life, to serve, and to be reconciled with his parents. When he finally met his future wife, he said, "Thank God for those years of delay. Otherwise the person I was back then wasn't ready to be a husband at all."

That tenth of a second in the AV node isn't wasted; it is there so that the next movement can be more powerful. God's delays are like that too. What are you waiting for right now? Perhaps it is not God's "no," but God's "not yet."

Here is another amazing thing: the heart's rhythm is generated by the heart itself; it doesn't need the brain to give an order every time. Nerves and hormones only speed it up or slow it down. That is why your heart beats faster when you exercise and slower when you sleep.

Also, people used to think that adult heart muscle cells never renew. A 2009 study using carbon-14 dating found that heart muscle cells actually do renew slowly: about one percent per year at age twenty-five, dropping to about zero point four five percent by age seventy-five. The exact rate is still being researched and debated. But it tells us that even the heart is being quietly renewed, little by little.

Electrical signals, delays, valves and muscle work together so precisely that the heart can keep working for a lifetime. That this points to purposeful design is a philosophical inference. But when you put your hand on your chest, it's hard not to sense the care behind it.
3. Guard Your Heart, and Receive a New One

Now we need to turn a corner. The Bible often talks about the "heart," but in the Bible, "heart" usually does not mean the physical organ. It means the inner center of a person: the source of our thoughts, emotions and will.
Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life. (Proverbs 4:23)

Just as blood flows out from the heart to supply the whole body, our words, actions and choices all flow out from within. If there's bitterness in the heart, our words come out with thorns; if there's gratitude in the heart, even our complaints grow fewer.
Not a Repair, but a Replacement
Our problems are, in the end, heart problems. And God's promise is not just a quick repair, but a brand-new heart:
I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. (Ezekiel 36:26)
What's the difference between a heart of stone and a heart of flesh? Stone is hard, cold, and doesn't beat; a heart of flesh is soft, warm and alive.
A heart of stone feels nothing no matter how many truths it hears; a heart of flesh weeps over other people's pain and is moved by God's love.

A heart usually doesn't harden overnight. It's like a riverbed slowly silting up, starting with just a little sediment. Once I'm misunderstood, and I tell myself, "Forget it." Once I'm left out, and I decide, "I won't give of myself again." Once a prayer isn't answered the way I wanted, and I think, "God doesn't listen anyway." Layer upon layer it builds up, until one day you suddenly realize your heart has grown as cold as stone.

We can't turn stone into flesh on our own. You can polish a stone and display it beautifully, but it's still a stone. That's why what we need is not a repair, but a replacement by God's own hand. Brothers and sisters, has your heart been slowly hardening? Maybe it's disappointment after disappointment, maybe it's the walls you built after being hurt. Today God says, "I will give you a new heart."
One of the two cores of 321 is "let Jesus reign." The heart is the throne of life; whoever sits on it rules your whole life. When Jesus sits on it, the outcome of our lives will be good.

If our heart is ruled by ourselves, by our emotions, or by money, the rhythm of life falls apart, like an orchestra with no conductor. Let Jesus be the conductor, and life becomes harmonious and ordered.

321 also teaches "920" (the nine fruits of the Spirit, lived out in relationships): live the self-emptied life in your relationships, and let the nine fruits of the Spirit grow from your heart. Fruit isn't hung on from the outside; it grows from within. When the heart is made new, the fruit comes naturally.

Finally, remember the order of relationships: God, self, others, tasks. Give your heart to God first, and your other relationships will fall into line. So often we rush to handle tasks and patch up relationships, but forget that the first step is giving our heart to God. Just as the heart's electrical signal must start from the SA node, the order of our lives must start with God.
This week: each morning when you get up, put your hand on your chest and say, "Lord, please reign in my heart today." Just one sentence, ten seconds, and it can set the rhythm for the whole day.
Brothers and sisters, your heart began beating before you were born and has kept beating until today. It doesn't need your praise or your reminders; it just keeps faithfully working.
And the God who made it is more faithful still. He does not slumber, and He does not sleep. When you are asleep, He is awake; when you are weak, He holds you up.

Now please place your hand on your chest again for one minute. With every beat you feel, remember one instance of God's care. And quietly ask yourself: lately, has my heart been a soft heart of flesh, or is it slowly hardening into a heart of stone?
Faithful Lord, thank You for keeping my heart beating until today. Every beat is Your grace; every breath is Your care.

Lord, take away the hardness in my heart and give me a soft heart that loves You and loves others. Sit on the throne of my heart and reign, so that all the outcomes of my life come from You. In Jesus' name, Amen.

The Guard Beneath His Wings: The Immune System, the Body's Guard
Yahweh will keep you from all evil. He will keep your soul. (Psalm 121:7)
Introduction: The Security Guard Who Knew Every Face

Peace to you, brothers and sisters! In the apartment building where I used to live, there was an older security guard downstairs. What made him so good at his job wasn't his strength, but his memory. The building had more than a hundred households, and he remembered which floor everyone lived on, what grade everyone's kids were in, and what time every grandma went out to buy groceries.
Once, a stranger tried to slip through the front door behind a resident. The guard took one look and said, "Sir, which unit are you visiting?" The man froze for a second, then turned around and left.

I've often thought that guard was a real treasure. But today I want to tell you that inside your body there is a guard force even better than he was. It patrols day and night, it tells friend from foe, and it remembers every encounter.
1. Two Lines of Defense, One Strong City

Every breath you take and every bite you eat brings in countless microbes. Sounds a bit scary, doesn't it? Yet most of the time you are perfectly fine. Why? Because an invisible guard is patrolling your body day and night.
This army has two lines of defense.
The First Line of Defense: Innate Immunity

The first line of defense is called "innate immunity." Skin and mucous membranes are like city walls, keeping most enemies out. Inside the walls there are also phagocytes, complement and inflammation, like patrols who are first on the scene, starting the fight within minutes to hours.
When you prick your finger and after a while the area gets red and swollen, that's not your body giving you trouble. That's the patrol arriving on the scene and fighting a battle!
The Second Line of Defense: Adaptive Immunity

The second line of defense is called "adaptive immunity." Here there are two special forces units: B cells make specific antibodies, and T cells recognize and clear out infected cells. They need a few days to prepare, but their attack is remarkably precise.

This unit uses a vivid comparison: the immune system is like a city. The walls keep most enemies out, patrols are ready to go at any moment, special forces deal with specific enemies, and the records office files away every enemy's face so it can be recognized at a glance next time.
God placed guards within our bodies; this is part of His everyday care. The Bible uses the picture of a mother bird spreading her wings to describe God's protection:
He will cover you with his feathers. Under his wings you will take refuge. His faithfulness is your shield and rampart. (Psalm 91:4)

Here we need to be clear: this is not a promise that believers will never get sick. Christians catch colds and end up in the hospital too. It is a promise that in health or in weakness, His faithfulness surrounds us like a shield, and He is with us in our going out and our coming in.
Yahweh will keep you from all evil. He will keep your soul. Yahweh will keep your going out and your coming in, from this time forward, and forever more. (Psalm 121:7–8)

Think about it: how many battles has your body quietly won this year that you never even knew about? We often think about our bodies only when we're sick, but rarely thank God for all the "days we didn't get sick."
2. An Army That Learns and Remembers
Memory Cells in the Records Office

The most amazing thing about this guard force is that it learns and remembers. After a battle, the body keeps "memory cells." The next time the same enemy shows up, the response is faster and stronger. Vaccines use exactly this principle: they let the body build a memory in advance, so it recognizes the real enemy right away when it arrives.

How long can this memory last? One study found that twenty-five to seventy-five years after smallpox vaccination, more than ninety percent of people still had substantial immunity. Of course, T-cell responses decline slowly, with an estimated half-life of about eight to fifteen years. But a single "training session" decades ago is still protecting you today. Isn't that astonishing?
There's another puzzle: we have a limited number of genes, yet the enemies out there number in the millions. How can we possibly produce so many different antibodies and receptors?

The secret is that as B cells and T cells mature, they reshuffle several sets of gene segments, like building countless shapes from a limited set of building blocks. Anyone with kids who play with building blocks knows that one box can become a car, a house, a dinosaur, with endless variations. God's design is truly ingenious.
This gives us a very important spiritual lesson. The body files away the faces of its enemies, and we too need to store God's Word in our hearts.

Why are some Christians carried away the moment they hear a claim that sounds right but isn't? Because the "records office" in their hearts is empty. Why can some people tell right away, "That's not right"? Because they have read the Bible for years, and the truth is on file in their hearts. When a lie shows up, they recognize it.

Every day we come into contact with all kinds of "spiritual germs." Some are a saying that sounds very reasonable: "All you need is to be kinder to yourself; you don't need God." Some are voices inside: "You've failed too many times; God won't want you anymore." Some are an article being passed around on social media that packages half the truth as the whole truth.

If there's nothing on file in your heart, these things will march straight in. But if your heart remembers, "For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life," then when the lie "God won't want you anymore" appears, your spiritual immune system will immediately sound the alarm: "No! I recognize this one. This is a lie!"

And just as vaccines are given during peaceful days, Scripture needs to be stored up during ordinary days. Don't wait until a crisis hits to frantically flip through the Bible for answers. Store up a little more in peacetime, and you'll have a little more strength in wartime.
3. Telling Friend from Foe, Just Right
A good army doesn't just know how to fight; it also knows who is the enemy and who is on its own side. As our guard force develops, it is trained not to attack the body's own cells.

And immunity has to be just right: too weak, and infections run out of control; too strong, or aimed at the wrong target, and allergies or autoimmune diseases result. The body has many regulating mechanisms that make this army both brave and restrained.
That a defense system able to learn, remember, tell friend from foe and exercise restraint reflects the wisdom and care of a Creator is a philosophical inference, but it is a very beautiful one.
The Church Is Also a Body
The church is also like a body. The Bible says:
When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. When one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it. (1 Corinthians 12:26)

Sadly, the church sometimes gets an "autoimmune disease" too: instead of fighting the real enemy, we attack each other. Over some small matter we treat our brothers and sisters as enemies and pour our energy into infighting.
Brothers and sisters, our real enemy is not the coworker sitting next to you, but sin, lies and the powers of darkness. The guard force doesn't attack its own, and neither should we.

And "just right" is also something worth learning. Some believers have too little spiritual alertness and swallow everything whole; others have too much, seeing heresy everywhere and sounding the alarm over the slightest difference, wearing out both themselves and everyone else. The immune system God made is both brave and restrained. When we discern right from wrong, let's ask God for that same balance: firm about truth, gentle with people.

One of the three foundations of 321 is "the Bible is my standard." Like immune memory, store God's Word in your heart, so you recognize a lie the moment it shows up. Reading a passage of Scripture every day is like adding one more file to your spiritual records office.

Second, 321 teaches us to have "235 comrades in arms," one of the three kinds of spiritual relationships. Don't fight alone. The immune system is a whole army working together, not a single cell fighting solo. We too need to find companions who pray for and remind one another, standing shoulder to shoulder in the spiritual battle.

Third, humility overcomes pride. Pride often makes us "mistake the enemy," treating people who disagree with us as foes and valuing our own face more than our brother's good. Only humble people can clearly tell who is foe and who is friend.

This week: find a comrade in arms, share one need with each other this week, and pray for each other. It might be someone in your small group, your spouse, or a friend in the Lord you haven't talked to in a long time.
Let's go back to that security guard. He could protect the whole building because he recognized every resident, and he could spot a stranger.

God has placed a guard force in your body even better than he was, and God Himself covers you with His wings. In your going out and your coming in, He keeps you, from this time forward and forever more.
Let's be still for a moment and reflect on one question: spiritually, can I tell the difference between truth and lies? How much of God's Word is stored in my spiritual records office?

Lord who watches over me, thank You for placing guards in my body that protect me day and night and win so many battles for me that I never knew about. And thank You for covering me with Your wings; Your faithfulness is my shield.

Help me store Your Word in my heart and tell truth from lies. And make me a member of the body who cares for others, not attacking my own, but supporting one another and fighting side by side. In Jesus' name, Amen.

2. Have you ever recognized a "lie" because God's Word was stored in your heart? Please share that experience.
3. How can the church avoid "attacking its own"? What is one concrete way you can care for a suffering member this week?
Grace That Stops Just Right: Blood Clotting, a Precise Chain Reaction
But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. (Isaiah 53:5)
Introduction: A Lesson from a Sheet of Paper

Peace to you, brothers and sisters! Have you ever cut your finger on a piece of paper? It's a strange kind of cut. It's just a thin sheet of paper, yet it hurts enough to make you wince. You go "ouch," watch a tiny bead of blood appear on your finger, press a tissue on it, and a few minutes later the bleeding stops. Then you get back to work and hardly give it another thought.
But today I'd like to ask you to "give it another thought." Because in those few short minutes, your body completed an incredibly precise relay race.
Not Too Slow, Not Too Fast

Think about it: if blood clotted too slowly, a small cut could bleed without stopping; if it clotted too readily, clots would form all through your blood vessels, causing strokes or heart attacks. Every day your body walks this precise tightrope.

It's like driving a car. Too little gas, and the car won't move; too much gas and no brakes, and you're in danger. What the clotting system has to do is have both an accelerator and a brake, and get the two working together just right.
How does the body stop bleeding? Broadly speaking, there are a few steps.
Step one: vessel constriction. The injured blood vessel first tightens to reduce bleeding, like turning down the faucet when a pipe bursts.
Step two: the platelet plug. Platelets stick to the break and cluster together, making a temporary patch.

Step three: the clotting cascade. A chain of clotting factors is switched on in sequence, each step amplifying the next, until thrombin is produced. Thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin, which weaves a net that holds the patch firmly in place.

And standing by is a braking system: antithrombin, protein C and other mechanisms confine the clot to the wound; once the wound heals, the fibrinolytic system clears the clot away. The job gets done, and then the work site gets cleaned up. What a thoughtful construction crew!
The Life Is in the Blood
The Bible told us long ago how precious blood is:
For the life of the flesh is in the blood. I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls; for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life. (Leviticus 17:11)
The life is in the blood. God protects our blood with such a precise system because it is life. Please remember this verse; we'll come back to it in a little while.
In 1964, Macfarlane, and separately Davie and Ratnoff, proposed that clotting is a "waterfall" or cascade of enzyme amplification, in which one molecule can activate many molecules.

This unit uses an easy-to-grasp comparison: clotting is like a row of ever-larger dominoes. The first small domino falls and knocks over a slightly bigger one, which knocks over a bigger one still, and very quickly a huge force builds up. But standing beside this row are many guards, making sure it falls only where it should.

Later, scholars proposed a "cell-based" model: clotting takes place on cell surfaces in stages of initiation, amplification and propagation, which better explains why clots form only at the wound. This model is now widely accepted, and the details are still being filled in.
Lose One Piece, and It Falls Out of Balance

How finely tuned is this system? If a single factor is missing, the whole system is thrown off balance. Hemophilia, for example, means factor VIII or IX is missing, and for such patients even a small cut can be very hard to stop.
This makes me think of serving in the church. Sometimes you feel like an insignificant little factor, as if it wouldn't matter if you weren't there. But in God's design, every link has its place.

There's a sister in our church who arrives early every Sunday, quietly setting out the chairs and filling the water dispenser. She often says, "I can't preach and I can't sing; all I can do is these little things." But once she went overseas for two weeks, and only then did everyone realize that the order and warmth before each service had been held up by her alone.

Brothers and sisters, don't underestimate your domino. The moment you fall may be the very push that moves the next person's life; the moment you're missing, the whole system may lose a little of its balance. In God's household, no one is superfluous.
A Question We Can Discuss Together
At this point I also want to share honestly that Christians and scholars hold different views on how the clotting system originated.

Behe argues that the clotting system is "irreducibly complex": without its key parts it cannot work, so it is hard to see how it could have evolved step by step. Doolittle and colleagues, comparing the genes of different animals, point out that jawless vertebrates such as lampreys have clotting systems missing some factors that still work, so they argue it could have formed step by step.

So what do we do? Our attitude is: unity in the essentials, charity in the non-essentials. Whichever view one holds about the mechanism, this precise system speaks of God's wisdom. Brothers and sisters don't need to argue about this in small group until they're red in the face; we can learn together and praise together with humility.
That a system able both to amplify rapidly and to apply multiple brakes points to intelligent design is a philosophical inference, and a deeply persuasive one.
3. Grace Within Limits, Salvation in the Precious Blood
God Sets Limits for the Sea
What God built into clotting is not only power but also limits. In the book of Job, God speaks to the sea like this:
and said, 'Here you may come, but no further. Here your proud waves shall be stayed'? (Job 38:11)
God set limits for the sea, and He set limits for clotting too. Stopping exactly enough, no more and no less: that is wisdom, and it is grace.

Our lives need limits too. Our anger needs limits, our work needs limits, and even our grief needs God to say, "Here it shall stop." God isn't trying to tie us down; He is protecting us, just as the brakes protect our blood vessels from being clogged by clots.

A brother who works in sales told me that he used to have no limits at work. His phone was on twenty-four hours a day; he answered messages during dinner and visited clients on weekends. His numbers looked great, but his family relationships were like a wound that kept bleeding. Then he learned to set limits for himself: phone put away at dinnertime, full attention to worship on Sundays. He said, "At first I was afraid I'd earn less, but I discovered that the limits God gave actually stopped what had been draining out of my life."
But brothers and sisters, there is a tremendous contrast here. Clotting stops our blood from flowing; yet Jesus poured out His precious blood for us, so that our sins could be forgiven.
According to the law, nearly everything is cleansed with blood, and apart from shedding of blood there is no remission. (Hebrews 9:22)

Remember what Leviticus said? "The life is in the blood." What Jesus poured out on the cross was not only blood, but His life. He did not have to go to the cross, but He went willingly; for our sake, He let His precious blood flow.
But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. (Isaiah 53:5)
Our bodies stop bleeding for us; the Lord Jesus bled for us. The first is God's wisdom; the second is God's love.
Let Jesus Receive All the Glory

One of the two cores of 321 is "let Jesus receive all the glory." That I am forgiven and healed is entirely because of His wounds, not because of my merit. Not one of us can say, "I was good enough, so I was saved." All the glory goes to the Lord who was wounded for us.

Second, lay down your life. Jesus shed His blood and gave His life for me; I learn to give of myself for others too. It might mean spending a little more time listening to someone, or setting aside my own rights so someone else can flourish. Laying down your life is not losing; it is following the Lord who first laid down His life for us.

Third, just the right measure. Just as clotting has both an accelerator and a brake, our words and actions need a sense of proportion, neither excessive nor indifferent. Some people are so overzealous that, like clots forming everywhere, they smother others; some are so indifferent that, like bleeding that won't stop, their relationships keep losing blood. Let's ask God for the wisdom to get it just right.

This week: in one strained relationship this week, be the first to say a word of forgiveness or apology, so the wound can begin to stop bleeding. Many relationship wounds keep bleeding simply because no one is willing to take the first step.

The next time you cut your finger on a piece of paper and watch that tiny bead of blood slowly stop, I hope you'll remember today: God designed a precise relay race in your body; and the greater grace is that His Son poured out His precious blood for you, so that you have peace and healing.

Please look at a place on your hand that was once hurt and has now healed, and remember how your body stopped the bleeding for you. And quietly reflect: Jesus bled and was wounded for me. What does that mean for my life today?
Lord Jesus, thank You for designing a precise system in my body to stop bleeding, with both power and limits, to protect my life.

And even more, thank You for pouring out Your precious blood for me. By Your wounds I have peace, and I am healed. Help me give all the glory to You, and learn to lay down my life as You did, being the first to speak words of forgiveness in broken relationships. In Jesus' name, Amen.

2. Facing differing views on the origin of the clotting system, how does "unity in the essentials, charity in the non-essentials" help you handle disagreements in the church?

Carefully Woven: Embryonic Development and Being Fearfully and Wonderfully Made
I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well. (Psalm 139:14)

Peace to you, brothers and sisters! Has anyone here ever worn a sweater hand-knitted by your grandma or your mom? I had one as a child. It was red, the sleeves were a bit too long, the neck was a bit too tight, and the color wasn't exactly in fashion. To be honest, back then I thought it was a little embarrassing.

Years later, when I was clearing out my closet, I came across it again, and suddenly I understood: my grandma had knitted this sweater stitch by stitch over many evenings, wearing her reading glasses. Every stitch held her time; every row held her love. A store-bought sweater might look nicer, but none of them was knitted "just for me."
Today I want to tell you that you yourself are a work carefully woven just like that. And the One who wove you is more patient, wiser and more loving than any grandma.
1. It Started with a Single Invisible Cell
A Beginning Smaller Than a Needle Point
You were once just a single cell, smaller than the point of a needle, only about a tenth of a millimeter across. If you put it on a table, you wouldn't even be able to see it.

Yet today your body is estimated to have about thirty-seven trillion cells. That's the 2013 estimate by Bianconi and colleagues, about three point seven two times ten to the thirteenth. Those thirty-seven trillion cells make up your bones, your heart, your eyes and your brain.
And it all began with that one cell.

Please raise your hands and take a look. Look at your fingers, your fingernails, the lines on the backs of your hands. These hands can write, cook, hold a child's hand and wipe away someone's tears. And yet all of this was once contained in that one cell too small to see.

Thirty-seven trillion is a number too big to imagine. We usually only hear the word "trillion" in news stories about national budgets. But your body holds thirty-seven of those, and every single cell is in its proper place, doing what it's supposed to do.

Imagine someone handed you a tiny seed and said, "This seed will grow by itself into a city, with roads, power plants, a communications system and a police station, all built by itself." You'd say, "You've got to be kidding!" But that's exactly what happened to you.
For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother's womb. (Psalm 139:13)
Before you even knew you existed, God was already at work forming you. Brothers and sisters, your story didn't begin on the day you were born.
2. One Recipe Book, Read in Different Ways
Next, let's look at how this amazing construction project unfolds. What follows is the general description found in embryology textbooks; each embryo varies slightly.
In week one, the fertilized egg divides into two, then four, forming a ball of cells that travels all the way to the uterus and implants.

In week three, three germ layers form. These three layers will later become, respectively: skin and nerves; muscle, bone and blood; and the digestive and respiratory organs. It's like building a house by first dividing the work among three crews: one for the outer walls and wiring, one for the structure and plumbing, one for the kitchen and ventilation.

Around day twenty-two, at the start of the fourth week, the primitive heart begins to beat. It is one of the earliest organs to start working. At that point many mothers aren't even sure yet that they're pregnant, but that tiny heart is already going thump, thump, thump.

Brothers and sisters, think about it: your heartbeat came before your name. Before your parents were even discussing what to call you, your heart was already beating. Before you learned to say a single word, your life was already reporting for duty before God.
By the end of week eight, the basic outlines of the major organs have largely appeared, and then the fetal period follows as the baby keeps growing and maturing.
One Recipe Book, a Thousand Readings

Here is something truly amazing. Every cell in your body carries the same "recipe book," your DNA. But heart cells open only the pages for making a heart, and eye cells read only the pages for making an eye. One book, read in different ways, makes a whole person.

It's like a big family's kitchen with a handed-down family cookbook. Mom turns to the braised pork page, big sister turns to the cake page, and dad turns to the fried rice page. It's the same book, but what arrives at the table is a whole feast.

Just think: if one day a heart cell got jealous of the eye cells and said, "I want to read the eye pages too!", that would be a problem. An eye growing in your chest? How would that person survive? Only when every cell faithfully reads its own pages can the whole body be healthy.

Isn't that also God's heart for the church? We all hold the same Bible and receive the same Holy Spirit, yet each of us is given different gifts and places. Some are given the pages on teaching, some the pages on caring for others, some the pages on quietly preparing the fellowship meal in the kitchen. There's no need to envy someone else's page. Read well and live well the pages God has given you, and the whole body will grow together.
There Is So Much We Still Don't Know

So how does a cell know where it is? What it should become? When to stop growing? Honestly, this involves complex signaling molecules and genetic switches, and it remains one of the most active research areas in developmental biology. How the embryo precisely controls the shape and size of each organ still holds many unanswered questions.

I really appreciate it when scientists are willing to say, "We don't know yet." It actually makes us humbler, and fills us with more wonder. That a single cell unfolds on its own into a complete human being, through precise and orderly steps, points to a Creator with a plan. That's a philosophical inference, but standing before such a vast mystery, it's hard not to think of the One who planned it.
A Poem from Three Thousand Years Ago
Three thousand years ago, the psalmist knew nothing of cells or genes, yet in the language of poetry he described the mystery of being shaped in the womb:

My frame wasn't hidden from you, when I was made in secret, woven together in the depths of the earth. Your eyes saw my body. In your book they were all written, the days that were ordained for me, when as yet there were none of them. (Psalm 139:15–16)

The word translated "woven together" carries the sense of weaving or embroidering in the original language. You were not thrown together at random; you were carefully woven. Just like grandma's sweater, every stitch holds love.
You have clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews. (Job 10:11)
Before You Were Formed, He Knew You
Even more moving is this: before you were ever formed, God already knew you.
Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you. Before you were born, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations. (Jeremiah 1:5)

Brothers and sisters, do you often look down on yourself? Not tall enough, not thin enough, not smart enough, not good enough with words? Just like I thought that sweater was embarrassing when I was little.

But the way God sees you is very different from the way you see yourself. He sees a work He wove with His own hands, finished stitch by stitch in secret. You are not a mass-produced factory product; you are handmade, one of a kind, woven on purpose.
There's another verse in the Bible that makes this very clear:
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them. (Ephesians 2:10)

"His workmanship" means you are God's own handiwork. God made you not just so you would exist, but He also prepared good works for you to do. You were not only woven; you are also sent. Your life has a design, and it has a mission.
From Man's Perspective to God's Perspective

321 teaches us to move from man's perspective to God's perspective. From a human perspective, my worth lies in my looks, my grades, my income, my performance; from God's perspective, my worth lies in the fact that God made me with His own hands and knows me.

These days it's so easy to live by other people's opinions. We post a photo and keep checking how many likes it has; we see someone else's life looking so exciting and feel like a failure. But the number of likes will be forgotten tomorrow, while what God has written in His book will never be erased.
This change of mindset changes a lot of things. You don't have to keep proving yourself, because your worth was written in God's book before you had lived a single day.

Second, people matter more than tasks. Every life, starting from the very smallest, is precious to God. When that cell in the womb was only a tenth of a millimeter across, God was already watching over it.

So we should look at every person around us the same way: the coworker who gives you headaches, the child who won't listen, the elderly relative growing frail. Each one is a work carefully woven by God. When we're busy getting ministry tasks done, let's not forget that people always matter more than tasks.

Third, give thanks in everything. Thank God for your body and your life, and be grateful to your parents for bringing you into the world and raising you. We often remember our parents' shortcomings, but rarely think about the fact that they gave us the chance to come into this world.

A sister shared that she used to start every day by looking in the mirror and finding fault: eyes too small, skin not good enough. Then she learned to start with a different sentence: "Lord, thank You for making me." She said the person in the mirror didn't change, but the way she saw herself did, and her whole morning's mood changed along with it.

This week: write a thank-you card to your parents, or to whoever raised you, thanking them for bringing you into this world. If they have already passed away, you can still write it down and thank God for them in prayer.
I still have that red sweater. It's still a bit unfashionable, and the sleeves are still too long, but I never think it's embarrassing anymore, because I know where it came from.
Brothers and sisters, when you know where you came from, the way you see yourself changes too. Now please look at your hands and your face, and say in your heart: "I was carefully woven by God."
And quietly reflect: do I often look down on myself? How is the way God sees me different from the way I see myself?
Lord who made me, I give You thanks, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Before I was formed, You already saw me; before I had lived a single day, You had already written my days in Your book.

Heal the part of me that belittles myself; let me see myself through Your eyes, and treasure every life, starting from the very smallest. Thank You for giving me my parents and the people who raised me. In Jesus' name, Amen.

New Every Morning: Wound Healing and Repair
It is because of Yahweh's loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his compassion doesn't fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness. (Lamentations 3:22–23)

Peace to you, brothers and sisters! Have you ever passed a subway station or a highway in the middle of the night? By day it's all rushing traffic, but late at night, when everyone has gone home to sleep, a different group of people appears: repair crews in reflective vests. They inspect the tracks, patch the road surface and replace the lights.
The next morning we go to work as usual, riding the train or driving, everything running smoothly, with no idea that someone worked there all night long.

Today I want to tell you that there is a repair crew like that inside your body too. And it doesn't just work the night shift; it works in shifts around the clock. While you sleep, it is still working overtime.
Three Hundred Thirty Billion a Day

Did you know? Your body replaces about three hundred thirty billion cells every day, weighing about eighty grams in total, most of them blood cells and cells lining the gut. That is an estimate combining multiple data sources.

You don't feel it, but this construction work never stops. Every day this many cells retire, and this many new cells start work. Your body today looks much the same as it did a year ago, but inside, many of the "employees" have been replaced.

Think about it: when you woke up this morning, did you say thank you to your body? Probably not. Usually the first thing we say is, "Ugh, work again." But while you were still asleep, your body had already quietly finished a whole pile of projects for you.
Some repairs we can see. You fall and scrape your skin; a few days later it scabs over, and a few weeks later you can hardly tell. Even a broken bone can grow back together.

When we were little, we often skinned our knees, and Mom would say while putting on the ointment, "I told you not to run so fast!" But before long the wound healed and we were running again. We never thought about how much was happening inside our bodies during that time.

Your body quietly renews itself every day, as if to proclaim that God's mercies are renewed day by day. Lamentations, as the very name tells you, is a book full of grief. Yet right in the middle of that grief, the author still says:
It is because of Yahweh's loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his compassion doesn't fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness. (Lamentations 3:22–23)
Every morning when you wake up, your body has quietly renewed itself a little, and God's mercies have been freshly prepared for you. Yesterday's failures don't have to be carried into today.

This unit uses a great comparison: the body is like a city with maintenance crews working in shifts around the clock. Some clear away rubble, some lay new roads, some inspect every electrical line and fix any damage the moment they find it. Let's meet three of these crews.

Wound healing broadly passes through three stages. First is inflammation, which clears the battlefield; second is new tissue formation, which fills in and covers over; third is remodeling, which strengthens the structure.

It's like a city after a typhoon: first you clear away the fallen trees and debris, then you patch up the holes, and finally you rebuild the roads even stronger. Wound healing is considered one of the most complex biological processes in the human body; we just take it for granted every day.

As kids, we all had a bad habit: once a wound scabbed over, we couldn't resist picking at it. As a result, a wound that was almost healed would start bleeding again and have to start all over. Mom always said, "Don't pick at it. Let it heal on its own!"

The wounds in our hearts are often like that too. God has already begun healing, but we keep bringing up old grievances and replaying that scene, tearing open the place that was about to scab over. Sometimes faith means being willing to take our hands off and let God repair us slowly, following His steps.

The second crew works in an even tinier place. DNA in the body is constantly damaged by processes such as hydrolysis and oxidation. Cells have several repair systems that check and mend it at all times.

Tomas Lindahl and two other scientists who studied these DNA repair mechanisms received the 2015 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Lindahl pointed out that DNA is in fact chemically unstable and depends on repair systems to stay intact.

Think about it: the "book of life" that holds the blueprint of your whole life gets letters worn away every day, yet every day someone carefully restores them, letter by letter. It's like a library where the librarians walk the shelves every day, and whenever they find a torn page, they mend it right away.

The third crew handles bones. After a fracture, first a hematoma forms, then a soft callus of cartilage and a hard callus of bone, and finally remodeling. What is rebuilt is real bone, not just a patch of cement slapped on.

Even more amazing, the process of fracture healing recapitulates many steps of embryonic skeletal development. In other words, when the body repairs a bone, it's as if it takes out the same manual it used to make bones in the womb and follows it all over again.

This reminds us that when God restores our lives, He also follows His original design. He doesn't just patch us up so we can barely get by; He rebuilds us according to the purpose He had when He first made us, so that we live the way He always intended.
He heals the broken in heart, and binds up their wounds. (Psalm 147:3)

The body has multiple built-in layers of self-repair, which reflects the faithfulness and care of the Creator. That is a philosophical inference, but it fits so well with the words of the psalm: the God who designed the repair systems is Himself the Healer.
3. Though Our Outward Person Is Decaying, Our Inward Person Is Renewed Day by Day

But we also need to be honest. Repair is not always perfect. Adult wounds often leave scars, while fetal tissue in early pregnancy can regenerate without scarring. About one in ten fractures heals poorly.

The body's repair is a grace, and it also reminds us that this body is still wasting away. We grow old, our hair turns gray, and our wounds heal more and more slowly. That isn't a lack of faith; it's that we live in a world still waiting for complete redemption.
Yet the Inside Can Be Renewed Every Day
And yet the Bible gives us a hope greater than bodily repair:
Therefore we don't faint, but though our outward person is decaying, yet our inward person is renewed day by day. (2 Corinthians 4:16)

The outer self wastes away, but the inner self can be renewed every day. An eighty-year-old may grow weaker in body day by day, yet his eyes can grow clearer day by day, and his prayers deeper day by day. That is what it means for "our inward person" to be "renewed day by day."
Wounds No One Can See, He Can Bind Up Too

What's more, God does not only repair bodies; He heals broken hearts. Some wounds cannot be seen: the pain of betrayal, the emptiness of losing a loved one, hurts we've been unable to voice for years. These wounds don't scab over and don't show up on an X-ray, but they are real.

I know a sister who, when she was young, was deeply hurt by the friend she trusted most. She said those years were like a wound that never healed; whenever anyone mentioned that friend's name, it felt as if her heart was being torn open. She tried forgetting, tried staying busy, tried pretending she was fine. None of it worked.

Then at one small group meeting she talked about it for the first time, and the group gathered around her and prayed. She said nothing dramatic happened that night, but from that day on, it was as if the wound had finally begun its "inflammation and cleanup." A year later she could talk about that chapter of her life calmly, and even pray for that friend.

Brothers and sisters, God says He "heals the broken in heart, and binds up their wounds." The wounds you can't see, He sees; what you can't fix yourself, He can bind up. There may still be a scar, but a scar can become a testimony, reminding you: it hurt here once, and God healed me here.
Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry
321 teaches us an important order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Let God restore my life first, and my relationships and service will be healthy.

Many people work incredibly hard in ministry, but the wounds in their lives have never been dealt with, so in relationships they hurt at the slightest touch, and in ministry they collapse as soon as they're tired. It's like a city that's busy putting up new buildings but never repairs the sewers; sooner or later there will be trouble. Let God restore you first, and your relationships and ministry will last.
Review and Correction: The Daily Spiritual Repair Project

Second, among 321's eight steps of changing our mindset are two steps, "review" and "correction." These are like a daily spiritual repair project. The body's maintenance crews make their rounds every day, and our hearts need a daily inspection too: Where did I say the wrong thing today? Where did I get angry? Where did I drift from God's heart? When you find it, correct it. Don't let a small crack become a big breach.

It's like brushing your teeth. No one says, "I brushed my teeth last month, so I don't need to this month." Spiritual review and correction is also a daily discipline, not a once-a-year spring cleaning. A little every day is much easier than waiting until there's a big problem to deal with.

Third, a wound has to be seen before it can be cared for. 321 teaches us to have "235 spiritual companions," one of the three kinds of spiritual relationships. Share your burdens with trustworthy companions, and let them pray for you and walk with you for a while. Many wounds never heal because we hide them and don't let anyone see.

Do you have one or two people around you to whom you can safely say, "I'm really not OK today"? If so, treasure them; if not yet, ask God this week to provide them. Healing usually doesn't happen alone in your room; it happens in relationships where people love one another.

This week: each night before bed, take three minutes to look back over the day, confess to God and receive His forgiveness, so every morning is a fresh start. Just three minutes, like the city's night-time maintenance, so tomorrow's roads can be safe and smooth.

Let's go back to that midnight repair crew. By day we enjoy smooth roads, but rarely think about them. In the same way, we enjoy healthy bodies every day, but rarely think about the God who watches over us around the clock.

Please recall an experience that once hurt you and has now gradually healed, and thank God for His healing. And quietly ask yourself: which wound in my heart still needs to be handed over to God to bind up?
Tomorrow morning when you wake up, please remember: His mercies are new every morning.
Lord who heals me, thank You for repairing my body day by day. While I sleep, You are still watching over me; in places I don't even know about, You are still mending.

Lord, heal the wounds in my heart as well. The ones no one can see, the ones I can't put into words, I place them all in Your hands today. Bind up my wounds, so that though my outward person is decaying, my inward person is renewed day by day. In Jesus' name, Amen.
