Hands That Work, Lips That Praise: Hands and Voice, Made to Serve and Praise
Let everything that has breath praise Yah! Praise Yah! (Psalm 150:6)

Peace to you, brothers and sisters! Let's start today with a little game. Everyone, please tuck your right thumb into your palm, and you're not allowed to use it. OK, now try using the other four fingers to fasten a button on your clothes, or pick up a pen from the table and write a word.
How did it go? Suddenly all thumbs, so to speak? Some of you have been fumbling with that button for ages, some of you keep dropping the pen, and the people next to you are already laughing.
OK, now let your thumb out and try again. Just like that, it's done!

Friends, we do thousands of things with our hands every day, but we rarely stop to think how amazing they are. Today is the last stop in our Human Body Hall. We're going to look at the hands and voice God has given us, and ask a very important question: why did God give us these hands and this mouth?
1. An All-Purpose Toolbox: Hands That Work

One hand has twenty-seven bones, including eight carpal bones, five metacarpal bones and fourteen phalanges. Put together, these twenty-seven bones can thread a needle and lift heavy loads; they can write and play the piano, and they can help up someone who has fallen.

Our little game has already given us part of the answer: the human thumb can meet the pads of the other fingers. This is called the "opposable thumb." With it, we can pinch, turn and hold with fine control.
Two Kinds of Grip, One Pair of Hands
The anatomist Napier divided human gripping into two kinds: one is the "power grip," like holding a hammer; the other is the "precision grip," like holding a pen. The human hand has both.

This unit says the hand is like an all-purpose toolbox: the same set of tools can do heavy work and delicate work. In the morning you use it to move boxes, in the afternoon to embroider; one minute it's hammering a nail, the next it's stroking a child's head.

The human ability to grip makes tools, art and caring for others possible. Think about it: every craft, every painting, every act of nursing care and every hug in human history has needed these hands.
Establish the Work of Our Hands
So why did God give us these hands? Moses prayed like this:
Let the favor of the Lord our God be on us. Establish the work of our hands for us. Yes, establish the work of our hands. (Psalm 90:17)
Our hands and mouths are not accidental accessories; they are for responding to God's love. Paul also says:
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them. (Ephesians 2:10)

Notice that we are "his workmanship," made by God's own hands; and God made us "for good works." God made our hands with His own hands so that we would use them to do good. A homemaker cooking a meal, an engineer writing code, a nurse turning a patient, a brother setting up chairs at church: as long as it is done for God and for others, it is one of the good works God prepared for us to walk in.
2. A Pipe Organ: A Mouth That Speaks
One Sentence, More Than a Hundred Muscles

Now let's look at the voice. To say a single sentence, you coordinate more than a hundred muscles of the larynx, mouth, face and breathing; Simonyan and Horwitz point this out. And it happens so fast that you are not even aware of it.
When you just said "good morning" to the person next to you, more than a hundred muscles performed a precise ensemble piece, and you didn't feel tired in the least.
The whole voice system works like this: the lungs supply airflow, the vocal cords vibrate to make sound, and the tongue, lips and palate shape the sound into words.

This unit uses a beautiful comparison: the voice is like a pipe organ. As air flows through different pipes and stops, it plays an endless variety of musical phrases. Your lungs are the bellows, your vocal cords are the reeds, and your tongue and lips are the stops. Everyone's pipe organ is different, which is why the moment you open your mouth, your mom in the next room knows it's you.

Even more amazing is language. With a limited number of words, people can build an infinite number of sentences that have never been spoken before. The sentence I'm saying right now may never have been said word for word by anyone in the world, yet you understand it immediately.

Linguists also debate what is unique about human language. Hauser, Chomsky and Fitch suggest that the ability to combine words layer upon layer into infinitely many sentences may be the core feature of human language; this view is still under discussion among scholars. Either way, being able to speak and communicate is an enormous gift.

That humans have been given hands and mouths able to create, communicate and praise points to a Creator who wants a relationship with us. That's a philosophical inference. But why would a God who didn't want to talk with us give us a mouth that can talk?
So what is the most beautiful use of this mouth?
Through him, then, let's offer up a sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of lips which proclaim allegiance to his name. (Hebrews 13:15)
Lips bear fruit. Some people's lips bear complaints, criticism and lies; other people's lips bear thanks, blessing and praise.

There's an older lady who works as a cleaner, and every day she hums hymns as she sweeps. Someone asked her, "Your work is so hard. How can you still sing?" She smiled and said, "My hands are sweeping and my mouth is praising. Both of them are serving the Lord!" That is a life in which hands and mouth are offered up together. Brothers and sisters, if we use such a precise ensemble of more than a hundred muscles only for complaining, isn't that a terrible waste? God gave us a pipe organ so that we would play songs of praise.
3. Offer Your Whole Body to Him

Now that we've walked through the whole Human Body Hall, let's look back together. We've seen eyes that can see light, a brain that thinks, a heart that never rests, blood that stops bleeding with precision, a guard force that patrols day and night, a life woven from a single cell, a repair crew that works overtime every day, and today, hands that work and a mouth that praises.
Eyes, brain, heart, blood, hands and mouth are all gifts from God. So what is the most fitting response? To offer our whole body to Him.
Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service. (Romans 12:1)

"Your spiritual service": that is, the fitting, reasonable response. That is worth pondering. When we truly see what a wonderful gift this body is, offering it back to the Giver is no longer a grudging duty; it is simply the only fitting response.

Or don't you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God's. (1 Corinthians 6:19–20)

This body was made by God, and it was bought back by the Lord Jesus at a great price. We are not our own. So what we look at with our eyes, what we think about with our minds, what we love with our hearts, what we do with our hands and what we say with our mouths can all become opportunities to glorify God.
Let Jesus Receive All the Glory

One of the two cores of 321 is "let Jesus receive all the glory." The skill of our hands and the power of our mouths are gifts; all we accomplish belongs to Him. You can play the piano, cook, fix things, speak well; when others praise you, don't forget to say in your heart, "Lord, You gave me this. The glory goes to You."

One of 321's aims is to "build God's kingdom system." How do we build it? It starts with these hands. Use my hands to serve in my family, workplace and church, so that God's purposes are fulfilled. God's kingdom system is not a visible building; it is built by countless hands willing to serve, working together.

Finally, become an overcomer. An overcomer doesn't only win in big things; an overcomer offers the body as a living sacrifice, serving with the hands and praising with the mouth every day. Every day, choosing to let your hands bless others and your mouth praise God: that is the overcoming life.

This week: use your hands this week to do one concrete act of service for someone, and use your mouth to speak a word of blessing to them. It might be carrying a bag for a neighbor and then saying, "God bless you." Simple, but powerful.

Congratulations on completing the Human Body Hall! From eyes that see the light to a voice that lifts up praise, we have seen that we are fearfully and wonderfully made, and we have come to know the God who made us with His own hands and watches over us every day.

Let's go back to the little game at the beginning. Without our thumbs, we couldn't even fasten a button. Life without God is actually like that: it may look as if we have everything, yet we're always missing that one crucial finger.

Now I invite everyone to lift up both hands together and use your voice to read this line aloud: "Let everything that has breath praise Yah! Praise Yah!" Then quietly reflect: what did my hands do this week? What did my mouth say? Did they glorify God and bless others?
Lord who made me, thank You for giving me hands that can work and a mouth that can speak. Thank You that throughout this Human Body Hall You have let me see that I am fearfully and wonderfully made.
Today I offer You my eyes, my mind, my heart, my hands and my mouth. May all the work and words of my life become a sacrifice of praise to You. In Jesus' name, Amen.
